hello.en: ¡Hola, mijo! I'm Tía Lupe. I'll teach you the Spanish we actually speak in Texas: at the carne asada, at the plant, at your wela's kitchen table. Textbook Spanish is good. Tejano Spanish gets you invited back.
hello.es: ¡Hola, mijo! Soy la Tía Lupe. Te enseño el español que de veras hablamos en Texas.

tia.en: First thing: say hi to everybody in the room, especially the viejitos. In Texas you don't walk past people.

tip.en: The everyday Texas hello. The answer is usually 'Nada, aquí nomás.'
Literally 'what happened?', but in Texas it's mostly just a greeting: '¿Qué pasó, primo?'
Use '¿Cómo está usted?' with elders and people you just met.
'Nomás' (just) is pure norteño and Tejano. You'll hear it all day.
Said with a shrug. Not great, not bad, still going.
Órale is a Swiss Army knife: okay, let's go, wow, or come on. Tone does the work.
The respectful way to answer when a parent or elder calls you. Never '¿Qué?' to your wela.
The classic Tejano way to wrap up a phone call: '¡Ándale pues, bye!'
Chicano and Tex-Mex, from English 'watch'. Friends only.
Safe with anybody. 'Ahí nos vidrios' is the joking version.

tia.en: In a Tejano family everybody is your tía or your primo, even if nobody can explain how. Just go with it.

tip.en: From abuela → buela → wela. Welo is grandpa.
Also güelo or buelo, depending on the family.
Mijo and mija come from 'mi hijo, mi hija'. Any elder can call you mijo.
Not niña (girl)! In South Texas, nina = madrina and nino = padrino.
Your child's godfather, or the father of your godchild. Family by choice, for life.
Texans call close friends primo too. Real cousins and 'cousins' are both welcome.
Huerco is the norteño and Texas word for kid. Playful, a little rough.
Literally 'my little boss'. Which is accurate.
Ask about the family before business. It's not small talk, it's the point.
Sunday means barbacoa, a full house and nobody leaving before dark.

tia.en: Here's a secret: take an English verb, add -ear, and conjugate it like any Spanish verb. Park → parquear. Check → chequear. Text → textear. Teachers may frown. Texas won't.

items.en: I'm going to park the truck.

tip.en: Two Tex-Mex classics in one line: parquear and troca.
Mexico says checar, Texas often says chequear. Both work.
From 'quit': cuitear, cuiteé, cuiteó.
Textear works all over the U.S.

items.en: We need to mop the floor.

tip.en: From 'mop'. In Mexico they say trapear.
From 'push'. Handy when the troca won't start.

items.en: I'm going to cash the check.

tip.en: Cashear el cheque on Friday, pagar los biles on Saturday.
Lonche (lunch) and lonchar (to have lunch). The lunch truck is la lonchera.
Los biles: light, water, phone. Everybody's favorite word.

items.es: Hay que aplicar para el jale.
items.en: You have to apply for the job.

tip.en: Aplicar (apply) and jale (job) are everyday U.S. Spanish.

tia.en: If somebody's wela offers you food, you say yes. If you're full, you say yes smaller. That's the whole lesson. Okay, there's a little more.

items.es: Un taco de papa con huevo

tip.en: The South Texas breakfast taco, on a flour tortilla, of course.
Texas runs on flour tortillas. Much of Mexico runs on corn (maíz).
Slow-cooked beef on Sunday morning, with tortillas and salsa. Not the same as barbecue.
Picoso is the Mexican and Tejano word for spicy-hot. If they say 'nomás tantito', be ready.
The Texas summer survival kit. Ask for chamoy if you're brave.
Before Christmas the whole family assembles dozens of tamales. Somebody always just supervises.
Conchas, marranitos, empanadas, from the panadería, with coffee.
Pásame = pass me. Works for tortillas, salsa, and the remote.
'Bien' before a word means 'really': bien rico, bien picoso, bien chido.
Say it with a smile. They will still make you a plate to take home.

tia.en: Caló is old Chicano street talk, from the pachucos of the 1940s to your tío at the car show. Use it with friends. With your boss's mom, maybe not.

tip.en: Ese means 'that one', so 'that guy', so 'dude'. Esa for a woman.
A playful yes. 'Simón que sí' = heck yes.
The no that goes with simón. 'Nel pastel' if you're feeling extra.
Firme = cool, solid, legit.
Disbelief or disappointment: no way, bummer, come on.
From carne (flesh, blood): a brother, or a friend so close he might as well be.
Trucha means trout. Ponte trucha means be alert. Nobody knows why. It works.
Caló for a car, especially a lowrider.
Cantón = house, home.
Rasquache can be a put-down, or a proud Chicano style of making art from whatever you've got.

tia.en: Southeast Texas works in the plants, on the docks, in the shops. On the job, safety words come first, then everything else. Aguas means watch out, and you'll hear it fast.

tip.en: Mayordomo is the crew boss. El jefe is the boss in general.
Ponte = put on (yourself): ponte el casco, ponte los guantes.
Casquillo is the steel cap. No boots, no work.
Every plant drills this. Know where yours is on day one.
Fuga = leak. Get out, go upwind, tell someone.

items.std: Ya viene el paro de planta.

tip.en: Shutdown season: long shifts, overtime, new faces. Spanish on site keeps the English word.

items.std: ¿Hay tiempo extra este fin de semana?

tip.en: Este fin = este fin de semana, this weekend.
Aguas is the shouted warning. It has nothing to do with water.
The most important question of the shift.
Literally 'throw me the hand'. Also: échame un paro (do me a favor).

tia.en: From Houston to Beaumont to Port Arthur, we've got three seasons: hot, hotter, and hurricane. Learn these and you can talk weather with anybody's tío.

tip.en: Bochorno is that heavy Gulf Coast air you can wear.
El aire = the AC. Apaga el aire = turn it off (nobody does).
Hurricane season runs June through November.
Literally 'the light left'. Ya volvió la luz = the power is back.
Inundar = to flood. Houston knows this word too well.

items.es: Da la vuelta, no te ahogues.

tip.en: Never drive into flooded roads. A little water can float a troca.

items.en: Let's go to the flea market.

tip.en: La pulga: food, music, tools, puppies, everything. A Texas weekend institution.

items.en: We need to mow the lawn.

tip.en: Zacate = grass, lawn. La yarda = the yard.
Houston Spanish keeps 'la freeway'. Agarrar = to grab, to take.
Texans say la luz for the traffic light. Textbooks say el semáforo.

tia.en: Ay, mijo, now the good part. Tejano music, conjunto, cumbia, a dance floor at a tardeada. And yes, we're learning 'bésame mucho' properly. No more 'besume'!

tip.en: Te quiero is everyday love: family, partners, friends. Te amo is deeper, more romantic.
Bésame = besa (kiss) + me. It's also the title of the famous 1940 bolero by Mexican composer Consuelo Velázquez.
Te extrañé = I missed you.
Tejanos say it to partners, kids and sometimes the customer at the taquería.
Use '¿Quiere bailar?' (usted) with someone older or someone you just met.
Al = a + el. Vamos al baile, vamos a la pulga.
Afternoon party with conjunto or cumbia. Everybody dances, from huercos to welas.
Accordion plus bajo sexto, polkas and rancheras: the sound of South Texas.
The happy grito when your song comes on. Practice it in the troca first.
Chula, chulo = lovely, cute. Sweet with people you know. Not for strangers on the street.
